intro.title: 27 Firefighters Killed in a Decade: Two Systemic Gaps That Keep Burning
intro.lead: National Fire Agency yearbooks show that major fires fell sharply over the past decade compared with the decade before, yet the number of firefighters killed on the fireground has only grown.

transition: The causes of firefighter deaths are complex. For this report we interviewed Dr. Chang Hsien-ho, along with Lin Chang-chih, secretary-general, and Cheng Shao-shu, deputy chair, of the Taiwan Firefighters' Rights Association, to look at fireground entry rules, factory safety, staffing and daily duties, and ask how to learn from past tragedies, reduce risk and save lives.
title: Fires With No One Trapped
titleLabel: Fireground command should put firefighter safety first

title: Taichung Daya factory fire:
no one trapped, yet firefighters were sent in
taichung.body: At 1:45 a.m., a fire broke out at an illegally built factory in Daya, Taichung. **No one was trapped inside**, yet a squad leader sent two firefighters in with a thermal imaging camera to look for the source of the fire. Ten minutes later the building was fully engulfed, and both firefighters were killed.

first.before: Dr. Chang Hsien-ho, now a tenured associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University's Worldwide Campus, once wrote in
first.after: about a question a classmate asked him while he was studying in the United States in 2005. It has stayed with him ever since.

rest: At the time, a fierce apartment fire was about to burn the building to the ground. No firefighters went inside; they only sprayed water from the perimeter to stop it spreading. In class the next day he asked a classmate why they had not gone in to attack the seat of the fire. The classmate shot back: "Nobody was trapped. Why send firefighters in to risk their lives just to put it out a little sooner?" He was struck by how different this was from Taiwan. Just months before he left for the US, a fire had broken out at an illegal electrical factory in Sanxia, then Taipei County. A firefighter went in alone to look for the fire's source in a building with no one trapped, and did not come out alive.

profile.name: Dr. Chang Hsien-ho
profile.bio: Tenured associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University's Worldwide Campus. A former section chief at the New Taipei City Fire Department, he went on to earn his doctorate in the US and has taken part in major disaster research and response-policy planning in both the US and Taiwan.

afterPriorities: Dr. Chang stresses that when the risk to firefighters is likely to rise, commanders must assess carefully rather than rushing to shrink the fire or protect property. This order of priorities should hold from training through to the fireground, and firefighters should not have to pay for management failures that could have been controlled. Since Taiwan passed the three firefighter-rights amendments in 2019, neglecting risk assessment can lead to serious casualties.
On the experience of front-line crews in recent years, Cheng Shao-shu shared the account of an anonymous firefighter, nicknamed Chao, who narrowly escaped a factory fire.
quote: I once went into a factory with no one trapped. I heard an explosion and a rush of gas. I yelled run! We scrambled out on our hands and knees......

paragraphs: Years on, fireground risk assessment for firefighter safety has not fully changed even after the right-to-retreat amendment. But Cheng Shao-shu points to the 2022 Meifu warehouse fire, fought defensively, as a case where the risk assessment was more cautious.

Crews advanced slowly from outside. The fire burned for 21 days before it was out, and the stench hung over the whole neighbourhood. The commander withstood pressure from residents and local politicians, refusing to chase a quick knockdown and putting firefighters' lives first.

Firefighters on an aerial ladder putting out the smouldering fourth-floor cold store on the south side of the Meifu warehouse
meifu.caption: The fourth-floor cold store on the south side of the Meifu warehouse smouldered until the operator removed the sealed steel panels, letting firefighters finally reach the fire. Photo: Yang Chan-hua
